items.title: Frames & auto layout
items.description: Auto layout makes things resize themselves around their content. Learn it once and you'll stop nudging boxes by hand.

metadata.practise: Build a mini component library (Stage 05 checkpoint).
metadata.seoTitle: Figma auto layout for beginners: frames that resize themselves
metadata.seoDescription: Learn Figma auto layout: direction, gap, padding, and hug vs fill. Build a button and a card that resize around their content.

quiz.question: Which shortcut adds auto layout?
quiz.why: Shift + A adds auto layout to your selection.

quiz.question: What does "Hug contents" do?
options: Shrinks the frame to fit what's inside
quiz.why: It's ideal for things like buttons that should fit their text.

quiz.question: A paragraph won't wrap when you shrink the card. What's the likely cause?
options: The text is set to Fixed instead of Fill container
quiz.why: Fill container lets text adapt to the available width.

quiz.question: Where should the gap values come from?
quiz.why: Using the same few values keeps your layouts consistent.

items.title: Components & variants
items.description: Build it once as a component, use copies everywhere, and change it in one place. Variants keep the different versions together.

metadata.practise: Build a mini component library (Stage 05 checkpoint).
metadata.seoTitle: Figma components and variants: build once, reuse everywhere
metadata.seoDescription: Learn how Figma components, instances and variants work, so you can change a button once and update it everywhere.

quiz.question: What is an instance?
options: A linked copy of a main component
quiz.why: Instances follow the main component's changes.

quiz.question: What are variants for?
options: Holding different versions of one component together
quiz.why: One button can have types, states and sizes without ten separate components.

quiz.question: What are overrides?
options: Allowed changes on an instance, like text, that keep the link
quiz.why: Overrides let you adapt a copy without breaking its connection.

quiz.question: When should you detach an instance?
options: Rarely, and only when you truly want it separate
quiz.why: Detaching loses the link, so the instance won't follow future updates.

items.title: Styles & variables
items.description: Name your colors, text and spacing once, then use the names. Change a value in one place and everything follows.

metadata.practise: Build a mini component library (Stage 05 checkpoint).
metadata.seoTitle: Figma styles and variables: name it once, change it everywhere
metadata.seoDescription: Learn Figma color styles, text styles and variables, and why naming by purpose beats naming by value.

quiz.question: What's the main benefit of styles and variables?
options: Change a value once and everything using it updates
quiz.why: Consistency and speed come from reusing named values.

quiz.question: What are modes used for?
options: Switching a set of values, like light and dark
quiz.why: A mode swaps all variable values at once.

quiz.question: Which name is better for a color?
quiz.why: Names that describe purpose stay true when the value changes.

quiz.question: What should you start with?
options: A small set, like about five colors and five text styles
quiz.why: A small, clear set gets used. A huge one gets ignored.

items.title: Constraints & responsive
items.description: Constraints tell elements where to stick when a frame resizes. Together with auto layout, they let one design flex across screen sizes.

metadata.practise: Build a mini component library (Stage 05 checkpoint).
metadata.seoTitle: Figma constraints and responsive design, explained
metadata.seoDescription: Learn how Figma constraints and auto layout work together so one design flexes across phone, tablet and desktop sizes.

quiz.question: What do constraints do?
options: Tell elements which edges to stay attached to when a frame resizes
quiz.why: They're like pins on a corkboard.

quiz.question: Which is usually better for a card whose text keeps changing?
quiz.why: Auto layout adapts to changing content.

quiz.question: How do you check that a layout is responsive?
options: Resize the frame and see what breaks
quiz.why: Resizing quickly reveals problems.

quiz.question: Why set a maximum width on text blocks?
options: So lines don't become too long to read on wide screens
quiz.why: Very long lines are tiring to read.

items.title: Prototyping basics
items.description: A prototype links your screens so people can click through them. It's for testing the flow, not for showing off animation.

metadata.youllNeed: A free Figma account; a friend to test with.
metadata.practise: Build a mini component library (Stage 05 checkpoint).
metadata.seoTitle: Figma prototyping basics: link screens into a clickable flow
metadata.seoDescription: Learn how to link screens in a Figma prototype with triggers, actions and animations, and why a prototype is for testing flow, not showing off.

quiz.question: What's a prototype mainly for?
options: Letting people try a flow before it's built
quiz.why: Prototypes are for learning how a design works for people.

quiz.question: What is a trigger?
options: What the person does to start a change, like a click
quiz.why: Triggers start interactions. Actions define what happens next.

quiz.question: How does Smart animate decide what to animate?
options: By matching layers with the same name across frames
quiz.why: Consistent layer names are what let it connect elements between screens.

quiz.question: What should you prototype?
options: The flow you need to test
quiz.why: Focus on what answers your question.

items.title: Design systems 101
items.description: A design system is a shared kit of components, styles and rules, so a team can build consistently and faster. Start small.

metadata.practise: Build a mini component library (Stage 05 checkpoint).
metadata.seoTitle: Design systems 101: what they are and how to start small
metadata.seoDescription: A design system is a shared kit of components, styles and rules. Learn what's inside one, when to build one, and how to start with a mini system.

quiz.question: What is a design token?
options: A named design decision, like a color or spacing value
quiz.why: Tokens give design decisions names so they can be reused consistently.

quiz.question: Which is a cost of a design system?
quiz.why: Systems need care or they drift out of date.

quiz.question: What does a mini system for a solo project need?
options: A small set of tokens and a handful of well-built components
quiz.why: Small and used beats big and abandoned.

quiz.question: What belongs in guidelines?
options: When to use each piece, with do and don't examples and accessibility notes
quiz.why: Guidelines help others use the system correctly.

items.title: Accessibility basics
items.description: Accessible design works for more people in more situations: tired eyes, bright sunlight, one hand, a screen reader, a keyboard. Build it in from the start.

metadata.youllNeed: A free Figma account; your keyboard.
metadata.practise: Build a mini component library (Stage 05 checkpoint).
metadata.reviewCadence: every 12 months (ideas change slowly; tool names every 6 months)
metadata.seoTitle: Accessibility basics for designers: design that works for more people
metadata.seoDescription: Accessible design works for more people in more situations. Learn the four principles, a practical checklist, and quick ways to test your designs.

quiz.question: What does POUR stand for?
quiz.why: These are the four principles WCAG is organized around.

quiz.question: Why shouldn't placeholder text be your only label?
options: It disappears when typing, leaving people unsure what the field is
quiz.why: Visible labels stay put and are easier for everyone, including screen reader users.

quiz.question: A user navigates with a keyboard. What do they need?
options: A visible focus state showing where they are
quiz.why: Without a focus indicator, they can't tell what's selected.

quiz.question: Who benefits from accessible design?
options: A wide range of people in many situations
quiz.why: Ramps, captions and clear contrast help many beyond the original group.

items.title: Handoff to developers
items.description: Handoff is a conversation, not a file transfer. Give developers what they need, early, and keep talking.

metadata.upNextLabel: Stage 06, Pick a project worth showing
metadata.youllNeed: A free Figma account; a developer friend if you can find one.
metadata.practise: Build a mini component library (Stage 05 checkpoint).
metadata.seoTitle: Design handoff to developers: what to include and how to talk
metadata.seoDescription: Handoff is a conversation, not a file transfer. Learn what developers need, how to prepare your Figma file, and how to keep working together.

quiz.question: What's handoff really?
options: A conversation between designer and developer
quiz.why: Good handoff keeps talking, before, during and after the build.

quiz.question: Which is a state developers need to see?
options: Default, hover, focus, disabled, loading, empty and error
quiz.why: If a state isn't designed, someone has to guess it.

quiz.question: When should you first talk to developers?
quiz.why: Early conversation catches problems while they're cheap.

quiz.question: Why agree on names with developers?
options: So the design and code refer to the same things and stay in sync
quiz.why: Shared names make everything easier to find and change.
